projects.name: AI Portfolio Assistant
projects.summary: An AI assistant being developed as part of my portfolio. Its goal is to answer questions about my experience, projects and technical skills using a controlled knowledge base.
highlights: Iterative development towards a RAG-based system

details.overview: The project aims to transform a static portfolio into an interactive AI application where recruiters can ask questions about my professional experience, projects, education and technical skills.
details.problem: Traditional portfolios require users to manually search through multiple sections of a website or a PDF resume. The goal is to make this information accessible through natural-language questions.
details.approach: The system is being developed incrementally. The target architecture includes Retrieval-Augmented Generation, a separate knowledge base, vector search and LLM-based answer generation with source attribution.
details.technical_details: At its current stage, the application uses FastAPI as the backend, Jinja2 for server-side templates and HTML, CSS and JavaScript in the browser. It also supports Polish and English and has been structured for further AI-related development.
details.evaluation: RAG evaluation will be introduced after retrieval and generation are implemented. The plan is to create a manually curated evaluation dataset and measure retrieval quality, answer correctness and hallucination behavior.
details.results: The project is currently under development. The web application foundation and code structure required for the future AI components have been completed.
details.lessons: The project serves as a practical environment for learning how to design an AI application from architecture and backend development through data handling, evaluation, testing and deployment.

projects.name: Deep Neural Networks in Survival Analysis
projects.summary: A research project focused on applying deep neural networks to survival analysis. I implemented DeepSurv and DeepHit and then developed modified variants with an additional module for analyzing the importance of input features.
highlights: 10 training runs per model on each dataset
Evaluation using C-index and Integrated Brier Score

details.overview: My master's thesis focused on the application of deep neural networks to survival analysis using oncology datasets.
details.problem: One limitation of deep neural networks is their black-box nature. The project aimed to introduce a mechanism that makes it possible to inspect which input features were most important to the model and to determine whether this mechanism meaningfully affected predictive performance.
details.approach: I first implemented DeepSurv and DeepHit. I then developed modified versions of both architectures containing an attention-based module for estimating the relative importance of input features.
details.technical_details: Data preprocessing included handling missing values, categorical-variable encoding including one-hot encoding, standardization and splitting the data into training, validation and test sets. Experiments were conducted on seven oncology datasets.
details.evaluation: Each of the four models was trained 10 times on every dataset. Performance was evaluated using the C-index and Integrated Brier Score, including analysis of average performance and variability between runs.
details.results: The added module provided a way to inspect the relative importance of features and therefore reduced the black-box nature of the networks. Its impact on predictive metrics depended on the dataset: some experiments improved while others remained similar or became worse.
details.lessons: The project gave me hands-on experience with deep learning, survival analysis, model interpretability, large-scale data preprocessing, experiment design and rigorous model comparison.

projects.name: DiagnoseMe
projects.summary: A desktop prototype for preliminary symptom assessment and recommendations for further action. It combined a structured symptom interview with LLM-generated responses through the OpenAI API.
highlights: Structured symptom selection and follow-up questions
Dynamic prompt construction from user data
Application data stored in Azure SQL
Explicit disclaimer that generated output does not replace medical consultation

details.overview: My engineering thesis was a desktop prototype designed to support users in preliminary symptom assessment and choosing further action.
details.problem: The project explored how a language model could be integrated into a larger application where user input is first structured and enriched with additional context.
details.approach: Users selected symptoms from a predefined list and answered additional questions associated with those symptoms. The collected information was then transformed into a structured prompt sent to the language-model API.
details.technical_details: The application was developed in C# using WPF. Application data was stored in an Azure SQL database. Besides the AI-related diagnostic flow, the project also included additional features such as user management, stored history and appointments.
details.evaluation: The project focused on application-level LLM integration and data flow rather than developing a proprietary medical model or performing clinical diagnostic validation.
details.results: The result was a working prototype combining a desktop application, database persistence and an external LLM API. Generated output was accompanied by a disclaimer stating that it was not medical advice and did not replace consultation with a healthcare professional.
details.lessons: The project gave me experience integrating an LLM API into a larger application, constructing prompts from structured user data and connecting application logic with persistent storage.

projects.name: News Extractor
projects.summary: An independently developed academic NLP project for classifying events in Polish text and extracting information about event participants and details.
highlights: Comparison of SVM, Naive Bayes and Random Forest
Custom dataset prepared with Gemini assistance
Naive Bayes achieved the fewest errors: 24 out of 302 examples

details.overview: An independently developed project created for a Natural Language Processing university course. The system classified events described in text and attempted to extract information such as participants and event details.
details.problem: The goal was to combine classical text classification with rule-based natural-language analysis and compare several common classification algorithms.
details.approach: Text was represented using TF-IDF and classified using SVM, Naive Bayes or Random Forest. spaCy was then used for further Polish-language analysis including tokenization, lemmatization and dependency analysis.
details.technical_details: The dataset was prepared independently with Gemini assistance. After event classification, the spaCy-based part analyzed sentence structure in order to extract information related to the event.
details.evaluation: The models were compared on the same test set containing 302 examples. Evaluation included confusion matrices and the number of incorrectly classified examples.
details.results: Naive Bayes misclassified 24 of 302 examples, SVM misclassified 29 and Random Forest misclassified 46. Naive Bayes therefore performed best on this particular dataset.
details.lessons: The project gave me practical experience with classical NLP, TF-IDF representations, model comparison and spaCy. It also demonstrated the limitations of evaluating models on a relatively small, self-prepared dataset.
